lesson.menu_title: That Is a Fair Question -- Q and A Mastery
lesson.menu_desc: Field the difficult questions after a talk and say exactly how sure you are: hedging language plus the words of the hot seat -- curveball, loaded question, deflect, concede, caveat, rule out, push back, stand by, get back to, grill
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 29 -- That Is a Fair Question
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Maria Claudia Curimbaba | Lesson 29 -- That Is a Fair Question
lesson.grammar_point: hedging certainty in answers (it seems that / tend to / is likely to / as far as I know)
phases: The Words of the Q and A

listenings.text: After a presentation, most people are afraid of the wrong question. They are afraid of the question they cannot answer. In my experience, that one is easy. You say: I do not know, and I will get back to you by Thursday. The dangerous questions are two others. The first is the loaded question, the one that has the answer built into it, like: why did you lose control of the budget? If you answer it as it is, you have accepted that you lost control. So you take the question apart before you answer it: I would not say we lost control; it seems that two costs arrived in the same month. The second dangerous question is the one you can answer, but only in part. Here, people tend to give the whole answer anyway, because silence feels like weakness. It is not. The strongest answer is usually the one with a caveat: this figure is right, as far as I know, but it assumes that the exchange rate stays where it is. That sentence does not make you look unsure. It makes you look like the only person in the room who has read the assumptions.

Twelve years ago, at the end of a very good presentation, a board member asked me whether we could guarantee delivery by December. I had rehearsed the talk for a week, and I had not rehearsed a single question. I said yes. I said it in two seconds, because I wanted the meeting to end the way it had started. December came, and we delivered in February. Nobody remembered the presentation. Everybody remembered the yes. What I should have said was simple: December is likely, but it depends on one supplier, and I will know for sure in three weeks. That answer would have cost me nothing that afternoon, and it would have saved me a very long spring. Since then, I prepare the questions before I prepare the slides. I write down the ten hardest things anyone could ask, and next to each one I write what I know, what I do not know, and the one sentence I am not going to say.

extra_audio.text: First, you listen to the whole question without interrupting, even if you already know where it is going. Then, if the question is loaded, you take it apart and you push back on the part that is not true. After that, you say what you know for sure, and you hedge the part that is only probable. Next, you add the caveat that the number or the forecast depends on. Finally, if there is a part you cannot answer, you say so, and you commit to a date to get back to them.
